Stage 7b: when is "take the first ride" not a driver's best choice?

World model 3 · ride_world · San Francisco and Pune

In stage 7 every trained driver agent ended up doing what a plain driver does: take the first ride offered, at once. Stage 7b asks what the market must look like for a smarter driver to earn more, and gives the drivers richer minds: each has its own income target, shift length, pull towards home and cost per km, and can take any of up to 6 rides on its menu, decline, or drive itself to another area. The policy is a 591,000-weight attention network trained only inside the world model; the result is then checked in the simulator.

In short
  • Done: the agent beats taking the first ride in the simulator, on 6 of 6 unseen days in each city. Its drivers earn +0.50 ± 0.04 median fares per online hour more in San Francisco and +0.05 ± 0.01 in Pune.
  • The key was more riders than drivers. Pay schemes, private or batched menus and taking half the idle drivers off the road still left about one ride per menu, and with one ride there is nothing to choose. With demand x3 a San Francisco menu holds about 3 rides and the first is the best only 40% of the time.
  • When every driver uses the agent, more riders are picked up (San Francisco +12%, Pune +5%), but riders wait a little longer (+0.3 and +0.4 min).
  • Drivers who keep taking the first ride lose a little (-0.11 ± 0.02 and -0.01 ± 0.00 per hour). The world model got the direction of every effect right, but overstated the San Francisco gain (it predicted +0.88 ± 0.09).

How it was done

1. Separate paydriver pay apart from rider fares, 8 schemes, all paying drivers the same total
→
2. Probebranch one driver's choice in the world model: decline or each ride, 45 imagined minutes each
→
3. Pick a marketthe setting where choosing beats the first ride: half the idle drivers off, demand x3, per-trip pay
→
4. TrainGRPO in the world model, 25% of drivers on the agent, 40 rounds (stopped at 33)
→
5. Testround-20 agent in the simulator, 6 unseen days per city, 12:00-14:00

    The figures, explained

    1. The market: when do drivers have a real choice?

    What it shows

    • Each column is a market design, adding one change at a time from left to right (probe in the world model, 60 SF / 40 Pune branched choices each).
    • Top: rides on a driver's menu. Middle: how often taking the first ride was the best branch. Bottom: what a driver gains per choice by choosing instead.

    What to take from it

    • Until demand is raised, menus hold about one ride and choosing gains nothing beyond noise.
    • With demand x3 in San Francisco the simple rule 'take the ride that pays most per minute' gains about 0.3 fares per choice.

    2. Training in the world model

    What it shows

    • Grey: the old market (half the idle drivers off, no surge). Orange: demand x3.
    • Each point: the gain of the 25% of drivers on the agent over the same drivers taking the first ride, on 12 held-out starts (± s.e.).

    What to take from it

    • In the old market training never beats zero. With demand x3 it does by round 10 and levels off by round 20.
    • Rounds after 11 continue from saved weights after a reboot; training stopped at round 33 (GPU memory).

    3. The simulator test

    What it shows

    • Top: the gain of the agent's drivers and the loss of everyone else, per day (dots) and on average, next to the world model's prediction.
    • Bottom: riders and drivers when the platform offers single rides or every driver uses the agent, against every driver taking the first ride.

    What to take from it

    • The agent wins on every unseen day in both cities.
    • The world model is right about direction, too optimistic about the size of the gain in San Francisco, and too mild about the cost to others.
